etjFalsifier.concern: The mirror might carry ETJ/interim/planning-area polygons alongside adopted in-city zoning, which would fabricate zoning districts for parcels not actually subject to them.
etjFalsifier.ztypeDistribution: Pulled all ~400+ distinct ZONING_ZTYPE values from the layer. Every one is a genuine adopted Austin base-zoning code (SF-1..SF-6, MF-1..MF-6, CS, GR, LO, GO, NO, LR, LI, MI, CBD, DMU, TOD, PUD, AG, RR, etc.) with standard combining-district overlay suffixes (-CO/-H/-NCCD/-ETOD/-NP). No ETJ/interim/planning category values present. Stated precisely: this field is a combined base+overlay code, not a coarse type flag, so it does not itself prove absence of ETJ contamination — it's consistent with in-city-only content, not conclusive alone.
etjFalsifier.geometricSample: Sampled 500 random Travis prop_ids, ran a scoped dry-run for austin-tx, got 25 real matches. Pulled each match's actual geometry centroid from txgio_parcel and point-in-polygon tested against Austin's own authoritative `City_of_Austin_full_purpose_boundary` layer (not a proxy). Result: 25 of 25 inside the boundary, zero outside.
etjFalsifier.statedLimit: 25 of 25 is not proof of zero contamination — at that sample size the upper bound on a true contamination rate is roughly 10%. It rules out GROSS ETJ contamination, not a small fraction (5% of 255,705 would be ~12,800 wrongly-stamped parcels).
etjFalsifier.whyApprovedAnyway: The structural argument, not the sample, is what actually settles it: Austin's ETJ is not zoned by the city at all, so an ETJ parcel carries no ZONING_BASE value to begin with and cannot match the layer's PIP regardless of what polygons the layer ships. The sample is corroboration of that mechanism, not the primary evidence. Approved by doc-repo-26 on that ordering — if the structural claim about Austin's ETJ ever turns out wrong, the 25-of-25 sample does not carry the weight on its own.

haysChurnFinding.method: For each of Hays' 4 pre-existing cities, sampled 200 real baked prop_ids (adapter_key=node-facets:tier1, cityKey filter) from place_layer_snapshots, ran a scoped dry-run (--prop-ids-file) against current txgio_parcel, read listSize/matched-in-store/notFoundInParcelStore/noZoningPolygonHit.
haysChurnFinding.aggregateVsPerParcel: Aggregate reconciliation (dry-run matched vs baked target) looked healthy (~90%) — this MASKED the real shape, because new parcels backfill the count while old identities vanish underneath.

perCity200Sample.kyle-tx: 30.5% of sampled baked prop_ids gone from current txgio_parcel entirely (upstream reload gap); 19.5% present but no longer inside any Kyle polygon (centroid drift or PIP behavior against the new vintage); only 50% cleanly persist.
perCity200Sample.aggregateVsBaked: kyle-tx 92%, san-marcos-tx 91%, buda-tx 83%, dripping-springs-tx 103% (baked provenance keys: kyle-tx 22268, san-marcos-tx 21192, buda-tx 7597, dripping-springs-tx 4320 — no 6th city key present, doc-repo-26's registry-regression hypothesis falsified)

haysChurnFinding.crossCountyCheck: Same 200-sample method run against Bastrop (bastrop-city-tx AND elgin-tx, 400 total), Caldwell (lockhart-tx), McLennan (waco-tx), and Travis (pflugerville-tx): all four came back 99-100% clean (Bastrop 100/100%, Caldwell 99%, McLennan 99%, Travis 100%). Hays is the outlier, not the norm — the 2026-09-03 reload's identity churn is NOT systemic across the six counties, though this only rules out Hays being one of several; it does not by itself prove exactly one county churned (only 5 of 6 non-Williamson counties have been directly tested this way; Williamson is structurally untestable by this method due to its own R-account keyspace change, a separate phenomenon).
haysChurnFinding.consequenceForBake: Not destruction — orphaning. A bake keyed on prop_id mints snapshots for new identities and never touches the snapshots belonging to vanished ones. Nothing errors, no count moves, and the stale rows are indistinguishable from live ones. This is P-121 item 1's (parcel succession, scoped and unbuilt) live-magnitude problem, not something to fix in this lane.
haysChurnFinding.notPursued: Explicitly did not chase WHY Hays' reload behaved differently from the other five counties — out of CTX-A's scope per the operator/coordinator's own instruction; belongs to whoever builds P-121 item 1.

brokerageAuthFinding.discoveredWhile: Smoke-testing #634's canary (extension_public tier retirement) before shifting traffic, per this session's own canary-then-verify discipline.
brokerageAuthFinding.rootCause: BROKERAGE_EXTENSION_PUBLIC_KEY was the ONLY brokerage secret ever provisioned to cortex-api's Cloud Run service — confirmed via `gcloud secrets list`, BROKERAGE_OPERATOR_API_KEYS/BROKERAGE_API_KEYS have never existed in Secret Manager. brokerageAuth()'s `keys.size === 0` 503 gate ran BEFORE the session-JWT verification check. The extension key was load-bearing for an entirely unrelated auth path: it was the only thing keeping the recognized-key set non-empty, which was the only reason any session-authenticated (real logged-in) user ever got past that gate.
brokerageAuthFinding.blastRadiusIfShipped: Retiring the key without this fix would have returned 503 property_brief_api_unconfigured to EVERY brokerage request in production, including real session-authenticated users — not just the retired tier, not just API-key callers. The usage evidence used to justify the retirement (248 brief runs ever, zero since 2026-08-09) was a true statement about the EXTENSION's usage; it did not measure the coupling that determined the actual blast radius.
brokerageAuthFinding.caughtBy: A pre-registered falsifier: curled the canary directly with the old extension key at 0% traffic, predicting a 401 (the intended retirement behavior). Got 503 instead — a real signal, not noise, because the expected result was stated before looking.
brokerageAuthFinding.fix: brokerageAuth() and requireBrokerageAuthOrServiceToken (which had the identical bug independently) reordered to check for a valid session-JWT bearer FIRST, independent of whether any static key is configured. MCP service tokens confirmed entirely independent of this — a separate SERVICE_API_KEY secret, checked before loadBrokerageApiKeys() is ever called, never at risk.
brokerageAuthFinding.verificationLimitPattern: A behavioral smoke test against the canary (old key / anonymous / garbage-dotted-token, all predicting 503) turned out to be NON-DISCRIMINATING: the unfixed code produces the identical 503 for all three inputs via a different code path (keys-gate-first vs. session-check-then-keys-gate). Initially misread this as confirmation the fix was live. The decisive check was PROVENANCE, not behavior: read the running revision's container image digest by field name (not tag), queried Artifact Registry for every tag pointing at that exact digest, found the tag WAS the #639 merge commit SHA itself (not merely an ancestor requiring merge-base), and confirmed why that tag is trustworthy by reading the build workflow's own `docker build -t "${IMAGE}:${{ github.sha }}"` step — first-party CI provenance, not an inference from timing or 'built after the merge.' PATTERN FOR THE RECORD: when behavioral probes cannot discriminate between a fix and its absence, test provenance (what commit actually built this artifact) instead of behavior.
brokerageAuthFinding.sideEffect: The deploy also shipped two other lanes' unrelated work under an auth-gate commit message: CTX-B's Round Rock/Kyle/Waco setback reconciliation (9b4fd6b8) and R-02's Caldwell/McLennan clerk-portal registry fix (c9295ad6). CTX-B was notified directly (its own close had left this question open, routed through doc-repo-26) since it was owed the answer that its work reached production.
